papers_seen.author: Solis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and/or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate representation imitation, layer-wise mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, adversarial or generator-based sample synthesis, and architecture-aware adjustments—that is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and data strategies to meet deployment constraints. Empirical results show distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, but open problems remain around robustness, low-frequency behavior, teacher errors, data scarcity, and principled curricula for multi-source transfer.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, empirically effective toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. By transferring teacher behavior through output probabilities, intermediate representations, or structured signals and by combining distillation with data strategies and complementary compression primitives, practitioners can achieve large reductions in memory, latency, and compute while retaining most of the original performance. However, realizing these gains in real systems requires attention to data availability, teacher–student alignment, fairness and bias risks, and task- or hardware-aware design choices.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical Tool for Compression — Powerful When Combined, Limited When Used Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller students that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD spans soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention alignment, multi-teacher schedules, and many-to-many layer mapping. In practice, KD reliably improves student efficiency and often preserves much of teacher behavior, but it has predictable failure modes — e.g., propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to teacher–student mismatch, and dependence on data quality and augmentation — that require complementary practices such as student pretraining, careful teacher design, data augmentation, and hybrid compression (pruning/quantization).

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: The Practical Power and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable and practical approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and—in many cases—more deployable models. When combined with complementary techniques (pre-training of compact architectures, pruning, low-precision numerics, or data-free synthesis), distillation can retain much of a teacher model's performance while meeting latency, memory, or privacy constraints. However, the success of distillation is conditional on choices about teacher-student design, access to data or surrogates, and optimization strategies; awareness of these factors yields the most reliable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. Across vision and natural language tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, selective sample transfer, multi-teacher and data-free strategies—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving most of the teacher’s performance. Practical success depends on matching what is distilled to student capacity, managing data availability (including data-free or synthetic approaches), and addressing harms such as transferred biases or degraded rare-token behavior. A pragmatic pipeline mixes pretraining, representation-aware losses, targeted data manipulations, and teacher-aware design to achieve favorable trade-offs among efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. Across vision and NLP, effective distillation combines choices about what to transfer (soft outputs, features, relational signals), how teachers are designed or ensembled, and what data or surrogates are used. Practical pipelines increasingly pair distillation with architecture search, curriculum strategies, and distributed training to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. While distillation often recovers much of a teacher's performance, success depends on careful alignment of objectives, data complexity, and optimization procedures; open problems include principled handling of imperfect teachers, robustness and fairness under compression, and scalable privacy-preserving distillation.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression methods form a diverse toolkit for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of the performance of larger teachers. Research spans soft-label and self-distillation strategies, layer- and representation-level transfers, architecture-aware and task-adaptive compression, and deployment-aware approaches that combine pruning, quantization, and distillation. Empirical work shows that careful choice of distillation signal (logits, intermediate representations, or feature maps), alignment strategy between teacher and student layers, data augmentation, and optimization scheduling materially affects student performance. Practical systems exploit these design choices to compress large pre-trained language models, accelerate inference, enable heterogeneous-device training, or improve low-precision networks. Despite progress, open questions remain about principled objective design, sample efficiency under limited data, and theory connecting transferred representations to generalization.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, general-purpose approach for translating large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Across architectures, modalities, and deployment constraints, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher's performance; however, realizing those gains in practice requires matching the distillation formulation to data availability, model mismatch, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD encompasses multiple mechanisms—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate feature imitation, relational/attention transfer, and progressive module replacement—and is used together with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical evidence shows that, when designed for the teacher/student pair and deployment constraints, KD can yield compact models that retain much of the teacher’s performance; remaining challenges include capacity mismatch, limited or private data, and preserving robustness and fairness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Fernandez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce compute, memory, and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. KD operates at multiple levels — softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational or structural signals — and is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful choices about teacher preparation, student capacity, and data handling. Although KD enables practical deployment across vision and language tasks (including data-free and privacy-sensitive scenarios), its effectiveness depends strongly on design decisions and faces limits such as capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, and data or domain mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Research has extended KD from simple soft-target matching to a toolbox of representation-level objectives, multi-teacher schedules, data- and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with pruning, quantization, or architecture design. Empirical work shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance in practice, but success depends on choices about teacher preparation, student capacity, data availability, and optimization; open problems include principled teacher selection, handling limited or no data, robustness to teacher errors, and aligning compression with hardware and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Orr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation condenses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment under memory, latency, or privacy constraints. Techniques span soft-target learning, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational objectives, layer-mapping strategies, and data-centric adaptations (including data-free and few-shot regimes). When combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search, distillation produces compact models that often retain most of the teacher's accuracy; success depends on matching distillation signals to student capacity, handling mismatched inputs or modalities, and designing appropriate data or augmentation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Complementary Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, versatile approach for producing compact models from large teachers that enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD encompasses a family of techniques—soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention mimicry, layer-wise alignment, multi-teacher fusion, and data-free synthesis—that routinely yield substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD has practical limits (data and domain mismatch, student capacity gaps, and safety/robustness concerns) that make it most effective when combined with complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search, and robustness-aware objectives. Practitioners should treat KD as the core of a broader compression toolkit and adapt which knowledge is transferred, how teachers and students are aligned, and what auxiliary procedures (data augmentation, adversarial training, teacher design) are required to meet specific deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-level toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. Effective KD requires selecting what to transfer (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational signals), matching teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques. When applied with task-aware objectives, projector or alignment modules, and careful treatment of data and teacher preparation, KD yields compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints, though capacity mismatch and data limitations remain important caveats.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. While classic distillation focuses on matching teacher output probabilities, practical compression across modalities and tasks benefits from richer transfer mechanisms: aligning internal representations, selecting task-relevant signals, leveraging data augmentation or synthetic data when real data are scarce, and using adversarial or ensemble strategies to expose diverse and robust teacher knowledge. When combined thoughtfully these methods enable students that are much smaller and faster while retaining or even improving accuracy and robustness on downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD operates through multiple mechanisms (output matching, representation mimicry, and relational objectives), and when combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis, and teacher adaptation) it enables compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. KD is therefore best treated as a composable toolkit: powerful in practice but requiring careful choices about what knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or sensitive data.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: The Central, Practical, and Conditional Role of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible set of techniques for transferring useful behavior from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can meet deployment constraints while retaining much of the teacher’s utility. KD methods span soft-target matching, intermediate representation and layer-wise alignment, ensemble-to-single transfers, task-adaptive architecture search, and data-free or privacy-conscious pipelines. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that approach teacher performance across NLP, speech, and vision tasks, and that combining KD with architecture-aware compression or augmentation strategies often yields the best trade-offs. However, KD has limits: student capacity, the availability and quality of distilled data, and inherited teacher biases can all constrain outcomes. Responsible and effective compression therefore requires selecting the appropriate distillation signals, considering task and deployment constraints, and combining KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or fairness-aware objectives).

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Necessity for Deploying Large NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Beyond simple logit matching, modern distillation encompasses feature-level mimicry, teacher adaptation, task-adaptive compression, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and continual or online schemes to maintain performance over time or across domains. When applied thoughtfully—choosing appropriate teacher signals, intermediate-target losses, and deployment-aware architecture search—KD enables real-world use of large pretrained models in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, and Evolving Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core engineering and research paradigm for compressing large models into efficient students while preserving accuracy and desirable behaviors. KD encompasses soft-target transfer, intermediate representation alignment, ensemble-to-single compression, and complementary data- and architecture-aware techniques. When treated as a design problem—choosing which signals to transfer, how to align representations, and how to manage data constraints—KD enables deployment across resource-limited and domain-shifted settings, but open challenges remain in preserving rare-token behaviors, coping with imperfect teachers, and operating without original data.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central paradigm for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Research spans theoretical analyses of when and why distillation helps, practical methods for compressing pretrained language models, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, strategies to preserve robustness, and distributed/federated adaptations. Methods include soft-label matching, intermediate feature/attention imitation, many-to-many layer mappings, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-distillation. Empirical and theoretical work highlights gains in efficiency and deployment feasibility across vision and NLP tasks, while also revealing limitations related to data distribution, teacher quality, robustness, and low-frequency token coverage. Open directions include principled handling of imperfect teachers, domain adaptation during compression, robustness-aware distillation, and scalable distillation in distributed or data-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—language understanding, machine translation, reading comprehension, and large-scale distributed training—recent work shows KD can improve inference speed, aid domain adaptation, enable training without original data, and increase robustness. Combining innovations in layer mapping, feature-level transfer, online and data-free techniques, and teacher optimization yields the best trade-offs for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide a broad, practically oriented toolkit for shrinking large neural models while retaining most of their performance. Methods include transferring soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, adapting teacher or student architectures, using adversarial or data-free sample generation, and combining distillation with quantization or pruning. Empirical results across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks show substantial latency and memory gains; success depends on what signals are transferred, how layers are matched, data availability and augmentation, and the deployment constraints that shape algorithmic choices.

papers_seen.author: Soto
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students for deployment in resource-, latency-, or privacy-constrained environments. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while providing additional benefits such as implicit regularization, improved robustness in some settings, domain adaptation, and enabling training when original data are unavailable. A practical KD pipeline selects what to transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how to supply data (real, augmented, synthesized, or data-free), and how to align teacher and student architectures; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) typically yields the best trade-offs. Remaining challenges include handling teacher–student capacity mismatch, domain and distributional shift, optimization stability, preservation of low-frequency behaviors in NLP, and privacy constraints, which motivate hybrid, task-aware distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applicable paradigm for compressing large models and transferring knowledge across architectures, tasks, and deployment constraints. A range of KD variants—data-free, federated, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, intermediate-feature transfer, and architecture-aware compression—have been developed to address realistic constraints such as data privacy, limited communication, teacher imperfection, and task-specific efficiency. By matching the KD strategy to the deployment constraint (e.g., privacy, compute budget, domain shift, or paucity of data) practitioners can obtain compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource requirements.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Settings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in latency- or resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from larger “teacher” models or ensembles to smaller “student” models. Work in this area spans methods that match final outputs, intermediate representations, or relational structure; approaches that adapt teacher signals through meta-learning or task-aware filters; and specializations for settings such as vision–language, graph learning, federated or distributed training, and data-free scenarios. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance, but practical success depends on handling domain shift, architectural mismatch, heterogeneous data and devices, and the quality or calibration of teacher outputs. Important theoretical and statistical analyses have begun to clarify when and why distillation helps, but open problems remain around robust, privacy-preserving, and architecture-agnostic distillation for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from large, often expensive teacher models into smaller or more efficient student models. Research has developed diverse KD mechanisms — soft-label distillation, intermediate feature matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data-centric augmentations — and applied them across domains (vision, multimodal, language, graph, and generative models). Empirical work demonstrates KD can retain much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and theoretical and empirical analyses link KD to regularization effects (e.g., label smoothing and bias–variance tradeoffs). Practical adaptations address modality misalignment, low-resource data, robustness to adversaries, and task-specific compression. Remaining challenges include principled teacher selection, distributional mismatch between distilled and original data, and scaling KD to large multimodal and structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single training trick into a flexible, task-aware toolkit for compressing large models into efficient students suitable for real-world deployment. KD can transfer output behavior, internal representations, and relational or structural knowledge; it can be adapted to constraints such as missing training data, privacy, distributed training, and domain shifts; and when combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, pruning, task-aware layer selection) it produces compact models that retain much of the teacher's accuracy while meeting latency, memory, and privacy requirements. Practical use of KD requires matching the distillation strategy to the application constraints (what to transfer, which data to use, and how to align heterogeneous architectures).

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to obtain compact models that retain much of the performance of larger models. Beyond simple logits matching, KD enables transfer of inductive biases, task-adaptive compression, privacy-preserving model release, and synergizes with structural compression techniques to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints in real-world systems. This article argues that KD should be a central component of modern model-compression toolkits for deep learning and NLP, both in practice and in research directions.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones across modalities (classification, sequence modeling, generation, graph-structured data, and federated systems). KD’s strengths arise not only from transferring teacher logits but also from transferring richer representation-level, adversarial, and self-derived signals. However, distillation has well-documented failure modes—optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, and domain or device heterogeneity—that require specific remedies. Combining representation-level objectives, teacher-friendly training, self-distillation or teacher-free approaches, and careful data strategies yields more robust and efficient compressed models while avoiding common pitfalls.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Practical, Private, and Robust Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is often framed narrowly as a model-compression trick to shrink large neural networks. This paper argues KD should instead be viewed as a core engineering and scientific tool for practical deployment: it enables training with limited or private data, yields task- and domain-adaptive compact models, improves robustness and fairness, and transfers intermediate representations and attention patterns that standard supervised training cannot. We synthesize evidence from recent work to show how variants of KD—self-distillation, layer-wise projection, multi-teacher schemes, teacher annealing, and data-free distillation—address concrete deployment challenges in vision and NLP, and we derive practical recommendations for combining these techniques in real systems.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structured relationships. Across deep learning and NLP, KD enables deployment of performant models under latency, memory, and privacy constraints and is routinely combined with complementary compression methods. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features), how to align teacher and student architectures, the availability and design of distillation data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and training protocols that mitigate capacity and distribution mismatches. Open challenges include robust teacher selection, data- and domain-mismatch, and scaling distillation methods to heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations. Across modalities and tasks, distillation methods vary by what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate features, attention, or structural knowledge), by whether they rely on original training data, and by how the teacher-student relationship is optimized. Practical goals include reducing inference cost, preserving accuracy under domain shift, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, and improving robustness or fairness. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen transfer targets, training curricula, and data strategies can recover much of the teacher performance in compact models, and that meta-level and task-adaptive approaches further improve transfer effectiveness. Key open concerns are how to best align heterogeneous inputs or architectures, how to retain desirable inductive biases (e.g., for domain-specific tasks), and how to ensure reliable student performance without access to teacher training data.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Integrated Feature-, Data- and Robustness-aware Knowledge Distillation for Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from simple logit matching into a toolbox of complementary techniques. Empirical and theoretical work shows that (1) matching internal features often transfers richer representations than logits alone, (2) the choice of input-side interventions (e.g., data augmentation) substantially changes distillation dynamics, and (3) robustness, teacher quality, and sample selection must be addressed explicitly. I argue that effective model compression in deep learning and NLP requires integrating feature-level mimicry with careful input-space design, selective or confidence-weighted teacher signals, and robustness-aware objectives. This combined approach maximizes student performance while keeping models compact and deployment-ready.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. While classic distillation focuses on matching teacher output probabilities, practical compression across modalities and tasks benefits from richer transfer mechanisms: aligning internal representations, selecting task-relevant signals, leveraging data augmentation or synthetic data when real data are scarce, and using adversarial or ensemble strategies to expose diverse and robust teacher knowledge. When combined thoughtfully these methods enable students that are much smaller and faster while retaining or even improving accuracy and robustness on downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-level toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. Effective KD requires selecting what to transfer (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational signals), matching teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques. When applied with task-aware objectives, projector or alignment modules, and careful treatment of data and teacher preparation, KD yields compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints, though capacity mismatch and data limitations remain important caveats.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compression and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, multifaceted technique for compressing large models while often preserving — and sometimes improving — task performance. KD can transfer ensemble behaviour, provide regularization benefits, enable deployment under privacy or communication constraints, and be adapted to domain-specific and generation tasks. Practical KD implementations leverage ensembles, feature-level projectors, data augmentation, self-distillation, or data-free/federated protocols depending on resource and data availability. This paper argues that KD should be treated not only as a compression trick but as a general-purpose training paradigm with distinct theoretical and practical consequences for representation quality, robustness, and deployability.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not a mere optimization trick but a central, versatile toolkit for compressing large models into compact, deployable students. When treated as a system composed of complementary ingredients—teacher design (single, ensemble or multi-teacher), what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, relational information), how to obtain data (real, synthesized, or data-free), and deployment constraints (privacy, federated or on-device latency)—KD consistently enables strong trade-offs between efficiency and performance across vision, language, generative, and real-world production tasks. Realizing KD’s full potential requires representation- and layer-aware objectives, adaptive teacher–student mappings, careful handling of data scarcity or privacy, and integration with pretraining and other compression methods.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, empirically effective toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. By transferring teacher behavior through output probabilities, intermediate representations, or structured signals and by combining distillation with data strategies and complementary compression primitives, practitioners can achieve large reductions in memory, latency, and compute while retaining most of the original performance. However, realizing these gains in real systems requires attention to data availability, teacher–student alignment, fairness and bias risks, and task- or hardware-aware design choices.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central practical mechanism to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment in resource-, latency-, or privacy-constrained settings. Research has developed a family of distillation objectives (soft logits, feature/representation matching, relational/correlation losses), training schedules (multi-stage, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or distilled corpora, data-free queries) that, when combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), enable compact models to recover much of the original performance. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to map teacher and student representations, and how to adapt pretraining and task data to the student’s capacity; remaining challenges include domain shift, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency behavior in NLP, and privacy-aware distillation.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single training trick into a flexible, task-aware toolkit for compressing large models into efficient students suitable for real-world deployment. KD can transfer output behavior, internal representations, and relational or structural knowledge; it can be adapted to constraints such as missing training data, privacy, distributed training, and domain shifts; and when combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, pruning, task-aware layer selection) it produces compact models that retain much of the teacher's accuracy while meeting latency, memory, and privacy requirements. Practical use of KD requires matching the distillation strategy to the application constraints (what to transfer, which data to use, and how to align heterogeneous architectures).

papers_seen.author: Dean
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behaviors and internal signals. A broad family of KD methods—logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, multi-teacher aggregation, and data- or task-aware variants—has been applied across vision and language tasks. Practical deployment typically combines KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and requires attention to data availability, teacher–student alignment, and robustness or fairness concerns. Open challenges include principled handling of teacher errors, data-free distillation, and reliable transfer of robustness and fairness properties.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.
