papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What is Known about Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Existing practice spans matching teacher output distributions, transferring intermediate representations or attention, online and ensemble distillation, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches when original training data are unavailable. KD is typically combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and shaped by practical concerns—teacher–student capacity alignment, what and how to transfer, data availability or privacy, and robustness—which determine real-world effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Gates
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically effective approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD encompasses transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and relational structure; it can be combined with architectural compression (pruning, quantization, parameter sharing) and with data strategies (augmentation, synthetic generation, data‑free rehearsal) to meet deployment constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey remedy: optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatches, data or domain shift, and risk of propagating teacher errors require task‑aware design, complementary compression methods, and careful validation. When applied as a principled toolkit — choosing what to transfer, how to align representations, how to prepare or synthesize data, and how to integrate pruning/quantization — KD yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance while satisfying latency, memory, and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a multifaceted toolkit for shrinking large neural models while retaining much of their accuracy. Approaches include matching teacher outputs (soft logits), aligning intermediate representations or attention patterns, transforming architectures to be resource-efficient, and designing teacher–student curricula or multi-teacher aggregations. KD is applied across supervised, self-supervised, few-shot, federated, and privacy-constrained scenarios and is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align layers and capacity, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; when designed carefully, KD enables deployment of compact models for diverse NLP and vision tasks while exposing open questions about robustness, fairness, and distributional generalization.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or ensemble models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. It is used to reduce memory, compute, and latency for deployment, to enable low-precision inference, to protect privacy, and to adapt models across domains. Practical distillation methods vary in what is transferred (logits, features, relations), how teachers are chosen (single, multi-teacher, self), and how training is regularized (data augmentation, loss design, adversarial objectives). While distillation often yields students that outperform similarly sized models trained from scratch, mismatches between teacher and student, optimization difficulties, and domain/privacy constraints remain important concerns. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and language tasks shows that careful design choices (data augmentation, multi-stage distillation, private/noisy queries, and specialized losses) meaningfully affect student performance and deployment trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster student models suitable for resource-constrained deployment. A diverse set of strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and intermediate representation matching to multi-teacher ensembles, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-supervised or privacy-preserving protocols—have been developed to preserve accuracy, robustness, and modality transfer while reducing inference cost. Practical systems combine distillation with quantization, pruning, or architecture search to meet application-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-level toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. Effective KD requires selecting what to transfer (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational signals), matching teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques. When applied with task-aware objectives, projector or alignment modules, and careful treatment of data and teacher preparation, KD yields compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints, though capacity mismatch and data limitations remain important caveats.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Methods, Limits, and Complementary Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core strategy to compress large pre-trained deep models so they can be deployed in latency- and resource-constrained settings. KD variants—multi-teacher pipelines, layer-wise and task-aware alignment, self-distillation, and feature-level matching—enable small students to approach or match teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost. KD is most effective when combined with complementary approaches such as pruning and architecture search, and when adapted to domain or system constraints (e.g., federated or multi-device settings). However, KD is not a universal panacea: data heterogeneity, misaligned inputs between teacher and student, and inappropriate augmentation or feature transfer can limit gains, so careful design choices are required to realize practical compression.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single training trick into a flexible, task-aware toolkit for compressing large models into efficient students suitable for real-world deployment. KD can transfer output behavior, internal representations, and relational or structural knowledge; it can be adapted to constraints such as missing training data, privacy, distributed training, and domain shifts; and when combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, pruning, task-aware layer selection) it produces compact models that retain much of the teacher's accuracy while meeting latency, memory, and privacy requirements. Practical use of KD requires matching the distillation strategy to the application constraints (what to transfer, which data to use, and how to align heterogeneous architectures).

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies enable deployment of large pretrained models by transferring function or representation from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) ones. Across supervised, self-supervised, and data-free settings, KD methods exploit soft targets, intermediate representation matching, architectural surgery, and data or training-time modifications to improve student accuracy, robustness, or efficiency. Empirical results show that appropriately designed distillation can retain most teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in model size, precision, or inference cost; but effectiveness depends on choices of targets, data, and teacher-student compatibility. Open challenges include preserving rare-token behavior in distilled NLP models, mitigating bias transfer, and jointly optimizing hardware constraints and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring useful predictive behavior and representations from a teacher to a student. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, adversarial or data-free approaches, and online or federated variants that trade communication and privacy constraints against fidelity. Practical success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to manage imperfect or heterogeneous data and devices, and whether to combine distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., pruning or architecture search). While distilled students often retain much of a teacher's performance and enable deployment under latency or resource constraints, open challenges include preserving rare-token behaviors, handling domain shift and robustness, and designing privacy- and communication-efficient protocols for real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Capabilities, Best Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a comprehensive, practical toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in vision and natural language tasks. When designed as a system—selecting appropriate teacher signals, leveraging intermediate representations, using data-aware or data-free strategies, and integrating complementary compression techniques—KD often yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, distillation has predictable failure modes (capacity mismatch, optimization barriers, propagation of teacher errors) and open research needs (reliable data-free methods, robustness and fairness preservation, principled teacher selection). This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central engineering primitive for practical model compression, and it outlines evidence-based best practices and remaining research priorities to make distillation robust for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. Beyond the classic teacher-logit supervision, modern distillation covers feature-level matching, task-adaptive architecture search, multi-teacher transfer, and data-free scenarios. KD can be combined with pruning and structured sparsity, adapted for domain shifts, and used to transfer ensemble or task-specific knowledge into compact models. The choice of distillation target, the availability of data, and the deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, domain) determine which distillation recipe will be most effective.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Aware Tool for Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single compression trick: when applied thoughtfully it enables deployment of large models by producing smaller, faster students while preserving task performance and transferring useful inductive biases. KD variants—matching outputs, aligning internal representations, using multi-teacher or data-free schemes, and pairing with augmentation or architecture-aware design—address diverse deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, and domain shift). KD has demonstrable benefits but also concrete failure modes (teacher errors, data mismatch, capacity gaps) that require methodical mitigation and integration with complementary techniques such as pretraining, pruning, or data synthesis.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Figueroa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies condense large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or lower-precision students suitable for deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Research has produced a taxonomy of approaches—soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate/feature imitation, relational or attention-based losses, multi-teacher fusion, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates that properly designed distillation pipelines can preserve most teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling substantial gains in inference speed and memory; theoretical analyses attribute much of KD’s benefit to regularization from soft targets and the transfer of inductive biases. Remaining challenges include handling teacher–student capacity mismatch, preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors, operating without original training data, and designing adaptive, task-aware distillation signals.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Engine for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a heuristic into a set of principled, modality-agnostic techniques that enable deployment of high-capacity models in resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings. By transferring predictive behaviour and internal representations from large teachers to compact students, distillation preserves much of the teacher's utility while enabling large speed, memory, and communication gains. Recent advances show that combining representation-level matching, teacher–student co-design, data-free synthesis, and task-adaptive compression yields robust, practical pipelines for compressing models across vision, language, graph, and federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, general-purpose approach for translating large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Across architectures, modalities, and deployment constraints, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher's performance; however, realizing those gains in practice requires matching the distillation formulation to data availability, model mismatch, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Day
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Paradigm for Compression, Adaptation, and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best viewed as a multifaceted training paradigm that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Far from being a single trick, KD encompasses soft-target (logit) matching, feature- and layer-level imitation, multi-teacher and self-distillation schedules, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. When matched to task constraints—data availability, architecture mismatch, privacy needs—and combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource targets. However, practitioners must address optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatches, and domain-shift or low-frequency behavior to reliably deploy distilled models.

papers_seen.author: Archer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can preserve predictive performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its strengths derive from a variety of mechanisms — soft-label matching, internal-feature alignment, layer-mapping, and task-adaptive architecture design — and from being combinable with complementary compression techniques. However, realizing consistent gains requires careful choice of distilled targets, attention to representation alignment between teacher and student, and explicit handling of data-, fairness-, and robustness-related risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a toolbox of targeted interventions rather than a single recipe, and provides concise, evidence-based recommendations for practitioners compressing models in vision and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-ingredient approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and other modalities. KD operates by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from teacher to student, and is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods, data and augmentation strategies, and careful teacher–student design. While KD can preserve a large fraction of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, its success depends on handling data availability, architecture and capacity mismatches, teacher artifacts, and distribution shifts. Treating KD as a configurable system—selecting what to transfer, how to align signals, and which auxiliary techniques to apply—yields the best practical trade-offs between compactness and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large, high-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, more efficient models (students). Across vision and language, practitioners combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, architectural design, and quantization) and with strategies for scarce or missing data to obtain deployable models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical success depends on choices about what to transfer (soft targets, features, attention), how to align heterogeneous architectures, the role of pre-training for compact models, and mechanisms to preserve robustness and rare-token behaviors. Data-free distillation, multi-task or multi-teacher schemes, and targeted representation matching extend KD’s applicability to many real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Current Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and graph domains, KD has been adapted into many variants — matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, progressive module replacement, online/multi-teacher training, and data-free or privacy-aware pipelines — often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation targets, student preparation, and data strategies are chosen carefully. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness is limited by teacher quality, data availability or privacy, teacher–student architectural mismatch, and risks of transferring undesirable teacher behaviors. Practical deployment benefits from combining KD with complementary compression and data strategies, designing student-aware teacher signals, and accounting for robustness and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Multi-Purpose Tool for Compression, Adaptation, and Responsible Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a broad, practical toolbox rather than a narrow compression trick. Beyond shrinking parameter counts, KD can regularize learning, transfer intermediate and structural knowledge, enable model adaptation when data are limited or private, preserve robustness and fairness properties, and support cross-modal or modality-restricted deployment. Realizing these benefits in deep learning and NLP requires combining complementary signals (soft targets, feature/attention matching, and relational losses), adapting teacher schedules and layer mappings to student capacity, and integrating KD with data synthesis or multi-teacher strategies when original data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. KD enables practical trade-offs among accuracy, latency, privacy, and data availability by varying what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps), how it is transferred (layer-wise, channel-wise, adversarial), and which complementary compression strategies are applied (pruning, architecture search, quantization). When combined with techniques for limited or absent access to original training data, KD supports few-shot, zero-shot, and privacy-respecting workflows that make deployment feasible across modalities and resource constraints. Successful application requires selecting appropriate distilled signals and curricula, and often integrating KD with task- and architecture-specific methods.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Conditional Endorsement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are indispensable tools for deploying high-capacity deep models in resource- and latency-constrained settings. When combined with architecture-aware strategies, task adaptation, and data-aware protocols, KD recovers much of teacher performance while enabling substantial speed and size reductions. However, distillation is not a universal remedy: optimization difficulties, domain and low-frequency token mismatches, privacy or data-availability constraints, and fairness concerns require tailored remedies. Effective compression thus integrates KD with architecture search, progressive replacement, data-free methods, and fairness- and federated-aware training to achieve reliable, deployable students.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relations. A variety of KD objectives—matching teacher logits (soft targets), aligning features or attention maps, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and self- or multi-teacher schemes—have been adapted across vision, language, multimodal, and structured prediction tasks. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and which data to use or synthesize for distillation. Although KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, open challenges remain including optimization hardness, propagation of teacher errors, domain and device heterogeneity, data- or privacy-constrained settings, and preserving robustness under distributional shift. Effective deployment commonly combines KD with complementary techniques (pre-training students, pruning, quantization, or data augmentation) and task-aware design choices.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other learned structure. A broad family of techniques—soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and layer-wise alignment, multi-teacher and ensemble transfer, architecture-aware transformations, and data-free or generator-based synthesis—has been developed to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation often preserves much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, but effectiveness depends on choices about what is transferred, teacher and student architecture, data availability, and optimization. Practical pipelines combine distillation with complementary methods (pretraining of compact models, data augmentation, pruning/quantization, and task-aware objectives) and must address challenges such as capacity mismatch, domain shift, robustness preservation, and faithful transfer of rare behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of the teacher performance. KD spans simple logit-based supervision to richer representation-, relation-, and adversarial-level transfers and is used to enable on-device inference, multi-task models, domain specialization, privacy-aware releases, and data-limited deployments. Best outcomes arise when KD is combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), task-aware design, careful sample or synthetic-data strategies, and interventions for bias and privacy. KD has clear empirical benefits across modalities but also well-documented limits—sensitivity to data availability and heterogeneity, potential propagation of teacher errors or biases, and the need for architectural and optimization care—motivating principled adaptations and further study.

papers_seen.author: Archer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can preserve predictive performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its strengths derive from a variety of mechanisms — soft-label matching, internal-feature alignment, layer-mapping, and task-adaptive architecture design — and from being combinable with complementary compression techniques. However, realizing consistent gains requires careful choice of distilled targets, attention to representation alignment between teacher and student, and explicit handling of data-, fairness-, and robustness-related risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a toolbox of targeted interventions rather than a single recipe, and provides concise, evidence-based recommendations for practitioners compressing models in vision and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible set of methods for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can meet practical deployment constraints. KD yields strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks when practitioners choose appropriate distillation signals, address teacher–student alignment, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques. However, its success is conditional: student capacity, the quality and availability of data used for distillation, optimization dynamics, and inherited teacher biases can all limit outcomes. Effective compression therefore treats KD as a toolbox to be adapted to task requirements rather than a single recipe, pairing it with architecture-aware compression, data and sample strategies, and careful evaluation of robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a logits-matching trick into a broad set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from large neural teachers. Modern KD variants transfer soft predictions, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structure; they are combined with data-centric practices (augmentation, synthetic and zero-shot data) and complementary compression (pruning, architecture search) to meet real-world latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work demonstrates strong gains in NLP (notably transformer compression) as well as vision, graphs, and federated settings, while theoretical and empirical studies reveal optimization challenges, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional/heterogeneity limitations. Practical pipelines favor pretraining or progressive replacement, representation-level matching, task-adaptive data strategies, and awareness of privacy and robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Castaneda
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: An Integrated, Task-Aware Argument
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, practical engine of model compression for deep learning and NLP when it is applied as an integrated, task-aware system. By combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, targeted feature mimicking, data strategies (including synthesis when data are unavailable), and architecture-aware student design, practitioners can produce compact models that preserve much of the teacher’s utility while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD’s benefits are conditional: student capacity, data availability and complexity, architecture mismatch, and teacher artifacts limit outcomes unless addressed through deliberate pipeline choices and evaluation. This paper argues for a pragmatic KD-centered workflow and highlights key components and cautionary considerations for reliable compression in real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Leonard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compression, Generalization, and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a multifaceted technique that both compresses large models for efficient deployment and provides regularizing, transfer, and adaptation benefits beyond simple model-size reduction. KD can be integrated with architectural compression, multi-teacher training, and modality transfer to produce compact models that retain or even improve task performance while enabling deployment on heterogeneous devices and privacy-sensitive settings. However, KD is not a silver bullet: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and distilled-data artifacts can harm downstream behavior, so careful protocol design (multi-teacher aggregation, mixing hard labels, data-aware schemes, or data-free metadata approaches) and attention to internal-representation alignment are necessary to realize KD’s full potential.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transform large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or more private students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structured signals. Over the past decade these methods have evolved from logits-based soft-label transfer to a wide range of strategies including feature- and attention-matching, layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, data-free and privacy-preserving protocols, and adaptations for few-shot or federated settings. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation pipelines can retain much of teacher performance while substantially reducing model size and inference cost; however, effectiveness depends on what is distilled, student capacity, data availability, and practical constraints such as privacy, communication, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile toolkit for turning large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students. Beyond parameter reduction, KD provides learned regularization, enables transferring intermediate representations and relational structure, supports data-limited or data-free regimes, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Practical success requires choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, augmentation, and deployment constraints; remaining challenges include distributional mismatch, capacity and representation gaps, and preserving robustness and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. Research over the past decade has produced a wide array of distillation variants (logit-based supervision, feature and attention matching, multi- and self-distillation, data-free methods) and shown how KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet practical constraints. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both the strengths of KD (regularization, practical deployment gains, domain adaptation) and its limits (optimization difficulty, capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors), motivating a pragmatic set of design choices for robust compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single training trick into a versatile, context-aware toolkit that enables deployment of large neural models in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings. By transferring softened outputs, intermediate representations, or relational structure from one or more teachers into a smaller student — and by combining these transfers with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware adaptation, and data synthesis — KD makes it possible to produce compact models that retain most of a teacher’s capabilities. Effective use of KD requires choosing what information to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to handle data limitations or domain shifts, treating distillation as a design problem rather than a one-size-fits-all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural networks so they can run efficiently in production and on resource-constrained devices. Recent work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and that a range of complementary techniques—data augmentation, multi-teacher schedules, internal representation matching, layer alignment, meta-learning of teachers, and robustness-aware objectives—meaningfully improve student quality or transfer desirable properties. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on optimization, the choice of teacher/student architectures, and the distributional complexity of the training data. I argue that best practice for KD in deep learning and NLP is to treat it as a family of methods to be combined—augmenting data, distilling intermediate representations, leveraging multiple or adaptive teachers, and explicitly distilling robustness—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central practical mechanism to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment in resource-, latency-, or privacy-constrained settings. Research has developed a family of distillation objectives (soft logits, feature/representation matching, relational/correlation losses), training schedules (multi-stage, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or distilled corpora, data-free queries) that, when combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), enable compact models to recover much of the original performance. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to map teacher and student representations, and how to adapt pretraining and task data to the student’s capacity; remaining challenges include domain shift, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency behavior in NLP, and privacy-aware distillation.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, graph learning, and distributed settings, KD variants—soft-target matching, representation- and relational-level supervision, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or federated protocols—have enabled substantial reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Practical gains depend on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited, private, or heterogeneous data; consequently KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, and Context-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically proven approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. As a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD encompasses soft-targets, intermediate representation matching, attention- and layer-aware mappings, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and data-aware protocols (including data-free and few-shot variants). KD delivers strong efficiency–performance tradeoffs when paired with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, but its benefits depend on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to handle limited or private data. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central, adaptable component of compression pipelines while recognizing its limits and prescribing evidence-based design practices for robust, task-aware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. It is a practical toolkit used to reduce memory, compute, and latency for deployment, to enable low-precision inference, to adapt models across domains, and to support privacy-aware or federated settings. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and language tasks shows that careful choices about what to transfer, how teachers are configured, and how training is regularized materially affect the trade-offs between efficiency and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.
